title: String manipulation
specPoints: 2.2.3 **String manipulation**: length, substring, position/indexing, concatenation, upper/lower case, ASCII conversion
learn: Find the length of a string and access individual characters by index (from 0)
Extract substrings in OCR pseudocode (`substring`, `left`, `right`) and Python (slicing)
Join strings with `+` and convert case with upper/lower
Loop through a string character by character
Solve typical exam tasks: initials, username generation, palindromes, vowel counts
hook: A school generates usernames: first 3 letters of the surname + first letter of the first name + year of entry, all lowercase. SMITH, Jane, 2026 → `smij2026`. Every system you log into has done something like this to your name. Today you write it.

video.title: Strings are lists of characters
video.brief: 4 minutes. The word COMPUTER in boxes numbered 0–7. Highlight `[0]`, `[7]`, `[-1]`. Slicing `[0:3]` as a bracket that includes 0,1,2 — stop excluded, same rule as range. Show OCR's `.left(3)`, `.right(2)`, `.substring(2, 4)` on the same word, side by side with the Python slice. Then `.upper()`, `.lower()`, `len()`, `+`. End with a loop `for ch in word:` lighting each box in turn and a vowel counter ticking.

p: A string is a sequence of characters, numbered from **0**. `word = "COMPUTER"`: `word[0]` is `"C"`, `word[7]` is `"R"`, and in Python `word[-1]` is also the last character. `len(word)` is 8; OCR writes `word.length`.

explain.code:
word = "COMPUTER"            OCR pseudocode              Python
first three letters          word.left(3)      -> COM   word[0:3]  or word[:3]
last two letters             word.right(2)     -> ER    word[-2:]
4 chars starting at index 2  word.substring(2,4) -> MPUT word[2:6]
length                       word.length       -> 8     len(word)
upper / lower case           word.upper / word.lower   word.upper() / word.lower()
join                         "ab" + "cd"       -> abcd  "ab" + "cd"
after: OCR's `substring(start, count)` takes a **start index and a count**. Python's slice `[start:stop]` takes a start and a **stop that is not included** — so 4 characters from index 2 is `[2:6]`. Mixing these up is the common slip.

explain.code:
word = input("Word: ")
vowels = 0
for ch in word.lower():
    if ch in "aeiou":
        vowels = vowels + 1
print(vowels)

# OCR style, by index
for i = 0 to word.length - 1
    print(word.substring(i, 1))
next i

explain.h: Useful Python extras (fine to use in the exam)
p: `word.count("a")`, `word.find("put")` (index or −1), `word.replace("C", "K")`, `word.isdigit()`, `word.strip()` (remove spaces at ends), `word.split(",")` (into a list). `in` tests membership: `"put" in word` is True. Strings cannot be changed in place — build a new one.
`word = "COMPUTER"`. `word[0]` is "C" (counting starts at 0). `word[-1]` is the last letter. `len(word)` is 8.

simple.code:
word[0:3]   # COM  (0, 1, 2 — stops before 3)
word[-2:]   # ER
word[2:6]   # MPUT
# OCR: word.left(3), word.right(2), word.substring(2, 4)

keyterms.def: The position of a character in a string, counting from 0.
Part of a string, e.g. the first three characters.
`s[a:b]` — characters from index a up to but not including b.

try.title: 5. String manipulation practice set
instructions: Work through the string exercises. Aim to finish the 'substring' and 'loop' sections in this lesson.

check.fb: Index 0 is P, index 1 is Y.
The empty string has no characters.
Python method call; OCR writes .upper without brackets.

exam.q: A program stores a product code as a string, e.g. "JE-2026-TV". Write pseudocode or Python to output the four-digit year from the middle of the code.
model: `code.substring(3, 4)` / `code[3:7]` (1 for correct start index, 1 for correct length/stop).
exam.commentary: Count the characters carefully: J=0, E=1, -=2, 2=3. Off-by-one here is almost always from starting the count at 1.

exam.q: Write a program that asks the user for a word and outputs the number of characters in it and the word in upper case.
model: Input stored (1). Length output using `.length` / `len()` (1). Upper-case output using `.upper` / `.upper()` (1).
exam.commentary: Three quick marks. The length and upper-case functions must be the correct ones; `size()` or `capitals()` do not exist.

exam.q: Write an algorithm that takes a string and outputs it with every vowel removed. For example, "computer" becomes "cmptr".
model: Loop through each character of the string (1). Test whether the character is a vowel (1). Build a new string containing only non-vowels / concatenate when not a vowel (1). Output the new string after the loop (1).
exam.commentary: The 'build a new string' idea is the key: students try to delete from the original and get lost. Mention lowercase/uppercase handling for a stronger answer, though it isn't required for full marks here.

home: Write a program that asks for a sentence and reports: the number of words, the number of vowels, the longest word, and the sentence with every word's first letter capitalised. Test with your own sentence and with an empty input.

misconceptions: `substring(start, count)` in OCR vs `[start:stop]` in Python — students apply the wrong rule to the wrong language.
Trying to change a character in place (`word[0] = "X"` fails). Build a new string.
`.upper` vs `.upper()` — OCR has no brackets, Python needs them.
say: 'Write the word out in boxes and number them from zero. Every time.'
'Python slices stop *before* the number — same as range.'
